turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come on in and we'll get your numbers before the doctor. Shoes can stay on.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, umm, thanks. I was pacing around the lot because I hate being late, and then I was early. Figures.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): You're alright. Arm straight for me. Pressure today is one oh nine over seventy-seven. Pulse is seventy-six.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that too low? I get scared when the top number isn't way up there. It's barely over a hundred.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Temp on here reads thirty-eight point three celsius. Weight, uh, one fifty-two... no, hang on, wrong button, it's one forty-eight pounds.
[SEG0006] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): For the old slip, last time in March you were sixty-eight, pulse that was, and your last pressure was one-forty. She'll be right in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): A fever? Nobody said I had a fever. Is thirty-eight point three bad? I feel, I don't know, normal-ish.
[SEG0008] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I just read the machine. Doctor can sort that out with you.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hey, sorry about the wait. I saw the slip. What brings you in today?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my calves. They cramp up at night, both of them, and it's been going on about two months. I can't sleep through it.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both sides, at night, for two months. How often does it actually hit?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every night. I, umm, have to get up and stand or it just locks. They're pretty bad. My sister said it could be a clot and I haven't been right since she said that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): A clot is usually one leg, swollen, warm to touch, not both calves locking in bed. I'm thinking more along the lines of...
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): But what if she's right? Should I have gone to the ER? I almost did, like, at two in the morning.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): From what you're telling me, I wouldn't send you tonight. I do want your medicines and how much you drink. How much water in a day, roughly?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and she said thirty-eight point three, is that dangerous, am I actually sick?
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's celsius, so around a hundred and one, a low-grade temp. Not an emergency on its own. You don't look toxic. The water, though?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Right, sorry. Umm, one glass maybe with breakfast, then coffee. I don't like water, it tastes like nothing.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): So not much fluid at all. What medicines are you on?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The water pill. I always say lasiks, but the bottle says furosemide, twenty milligrams, every morning, for my high blood pressure.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Furosemide, twenty milligrams by mouth each morning. That can waste potassium, and if you're barely drinking, the muscle just cramps. Anything you picked up at the shop?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Magnesium, for the cramps. Magnesium oxide, four hundred milligrams at bedtime. I started it last winter, or the one before, I honestly can't tell you which.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Four hundred at night is a usual shop dose, I'd keep it for now. When a cramp hits, does the standing actually break it?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Standing, or I stretch on the wall, and it eases in a minute or two. Then I'm just awake, worrying.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any chest pain or pressure that comes with these?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Wait, if the water pill is doing this, shouldn't I just stop it? I don't want the pressure to shoot up, though, that's the thing.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it on your own. Twenty is not a huge dose, but I'm not changing it until we see the potassium. Chest pain, yes or no?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I kept thinking heart, but it's the legs.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): How about breathing, any cough, wheeze, that respiratory side?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. Breathing's fine. No wheeze or anything.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): And fever, chills, have you been feeling sick with this?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Well, I felt kind of warm last night, but I figured it was the heating. I don't really know.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): So that's muddy. I won't hang a fever illness on one warm night and one reading. Let me check the legs.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): They're quiet right now. Does that wreck the exam? I can try to, umm...
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): No need. Cramps come and go. Calves are soft, no redness, no swelling, and the pulses in your feet are good.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So not a clot? Please just say it straight, I'm gonna ask twice anyway.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I don't see a clot on exam. Working idea is nocturnal calf cramps, possibly from the furosemide plus not enough fluid, but I want the potassium before I lean on that too hard.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): And if the potassium's low, is that an IV? I read this thing online and it was, err, horrible.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Usually a pill or some diet changes, not an IV, unless it's truly dangerous, which nothing here suggests. I'm ordering a blood test for your potassium and the other electrolytes, today, before you head out.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Today, like now? Does the needle hurt, and where do I even go?

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lab's down the hall, one stick. Before bed, stretch each calf on the wall, hold about thirty seconds, both sides. Try for a couple extra glasses of water. Come back in about two weeks and we'll go over the numbers.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If it grabs me tonight I just stretch, I don't race to the ER, right? And I keep the lasiks and the magnesium both?
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Keep both exactly as they are. ER only if a leg swells up hard, or you get chest pain, or you can't catch your breath. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

omissions.text: Calf cramps wake the patient and she 'can't sleep through it'; after standing or wall stretching they ease within 1–2 minutes but then she remains awake worrying.
Standing is not the only relieving factor mentioned; wall stretching also relieves the cramps.
Negative finding discussed by doctor: no chills / not clearly feeling sick; patient said she did not think so, though she may have felt warm the prior night and was unsure.
Doctor explicitly stated he would not send the patient to the ER tonight based on the history given.
Doctor advised not changing furosemide until potassium results are available.
ER precautions were tied specifically to red-flag symptoms of a leg becoming swollen/warm concern, chest pain, or inability to catch breath; doctor also reassured that he did not see a clot on exam.
